docs.title: GuardSQL
docs.text:
GuardSQL is a small, application-neutral query language for SaaS analytics and reporting. It gives users a SQL-like interface without passing customer-authored SQL directly to a database.

The core contract is:

query text -> parse -> validate -> policy -> compile -> parameterized SQL + args

Untrusted SQL in, trusted SQL out: GuardSQL parses customer text into an AST, validates and policy-checks it, then regenerates parameterized, dialect-specific SQL from the AST — the original text is never executed. GuardSQL owns parsing, AST types, validation, policy checks, a built-in SQL compiler (SQLite/PostgreSQL/MySQL with JSON extraction), a trusted mutation builder, and a limited in-memory evaluator. Applications own tenant scope, authorization, execution limits, and audit logging.

This repository is the Go implementation of that engine. Language/runtime integrations should be separate from the root module. For example, a Hibernate adapter should live in a Java-oriented repository such as github.com/grokify/guardsql-java or github.com/grokify/guardsql-hibernate and consume the same conceptual AST/policy contract without adding Java dependencies here.

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
• Keep customer query text away from direct database execution.
  • Regenerate parameterized SQL from the validated AST, never pass user text through.
  • Make unsupported syntax fail as a normal parse error.
  • Validate entities and fields against explicit allowlisted schemas.
  • Enforce read-only and field-level policy against the AST.
  • Serve trusted internal SQL (including mutations) from the same hardened engine.
  • Keep the root Go module dependency-light.
  • Put heavyweight authorization integrations in optional modules.
  • Keep non-Go runtime integrations outside this repository.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
• Parser + AST for a read-only SQL subset.
  • Schema validation against an allowlist of entities, fields, types, and capabilities, with per-field data classification.
  • Policy checks for operations, limits, and query complexity.
  • SQL compiler — AST to parameterized SQLite / PostgreSQL / MySQL, including JSON path extraction.
  • Config & trust modes — hardened untrusted and trusted profiles with a one-step Compile.
  • Mutations — a trusted INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE builder.
  • Identifier lockdown — safe-charset enforcement for table and column names.

docs.title: Core Packages
docs.text: Package Purpose github.com/grokify/guardsql Parser, AST, schema validation, policy, evaluator github.com/grokify/guardsql/authz Lightweight authorization decision helper github.com/grokify/guardsql/authzsystemforge Optional SystemForge/SpiceDB adapter module

docs.title: Minimal Example
docs.text:
The high-level Config runs parse → validate → policy → compile in one call:

cfg := guardsql.NewUntrustedConfig(schema, guardsql.DialectPostgres)

out, err := cfg.Compile(`SELECT id, name FROM roadmap_items WHERE status = "planned" LIMIT 25`)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
rows, err := db.Query(out.SQL, out.Args...) // parameterized, dialect-specific

The lower-level primitives remain available for custom pipelines:

q, err := guardsql.Parse(input)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := guardsql.Validate(q, schema); err != nil {
    return err
}
if issues := guardsql.CheckPolicy(q, policy); len(issues) > 0 {
    return fmt.Errorf("query not allowed: %s", issues[0].Message)
}
out, err := guardsql.Compile(q, guardsql.CompileOptions{Dialect: guardsql.DialectPostgres, Schema: schema})

docs.title: Development
docs.text: GuardSQL should stay small and dependency-light.

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
.
├── ast.go
├── lexer.go
├── parser.go
├── schema.go
├── validate.go
├── policy.go
├── lint.go
├── eval.go

docs.title: Module Boundaries
docs.text:
• Root module: github.com/grokify/guardsql
  • Optional SystemForge module: github.com/grokify/guardsql/authzsystemforge

Do not add SystemForge, SpiceDB, Cedar, Rego, SQL drivers, Ent, or storage dependencies to the root module.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Run root tests:

go test ./...
go vet ./...

Run browser package tests:

cd ts
npm test

Run optional SystemForge adapter tests separately:

cd authzsystemforge
go test ./...
go vet ./...

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Build the docs locally:

mkdocs build --strict

The generated site/ directory should not be committed.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: The root GuardSQL module does not import concrete authorization engines. It defines AST and policy primitives. Host applications decide how to authorize principals and may compile those decisions into guardsql.Policy.

docs.title: Lightweight Decision Helper
docs.text:
The authz package defines a small decision shape:

decision := authz.Decision{
    AllowedEntities: []string{"roadmap_items"},
    Fields: map[string]map[string]guardsql.FieldPolicy{
        "roadmap_items": {
            "name": {Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true},
        },
    },
    MaxDepth:    8,
    MaxNodes:    80,
    MaxInValues: 100,
}

policy := authz.PolicyFromDecision(decision)

External engines should produce decisions from trusted application context, not from user-authored query text.

docs.title: SystemForge and SpiceDB
docs.text:
SystemForge integration lives in the optional nested module:

go get github.com/grokify/guardsql/authzsystemforge

Example:

policy, err := authzsystemforge.PolicyBuilder{
    Authorizer: provider, // systemforge/authz.Authorizer
    Principal:  authz.NewUserPrincipal(userID),
    Schema:     schema,
    ResourceBuilder: myResourceBuilder,
    MaxDepth:   8,
    MaxNodes:   80,
}.Build(ctx)

The adapter checks:

GuardSQL use SystemForge action Entity read read Select field read Filter field list Sort/group field sort

docs.title: Resource Mapping
docs.text:
Production SpiceDB deployments should provide a custom resource builder so query entities and fields map to concrete product resources:

analytics_dataset:<dataset_id>
analytics_field:<field_id>

Attribute-only resources are useful for tests and examples, but SystemForge's SpiceDB provider checks concrete type/id/permission tuples.

docs.title: Other Engines
docs.text:
Cedar, Rego, SpiceDB, Casbin, or custom RBAC engines can all be used by compiling their decisions into guardsql.Policy.

Keep heavyweight engine dependencies outside the root module. Use optional subpackages or nested modules when an integration needs non-trivial dependency graphs.

docs.title: Backend Execution
docs.text: GuardSQL is not a database engine. It provides an AST and helpers that backend providers can use safely.

docs.title: In-Memory Evaluator
docs.text:
Eval supports:

  • single-source filters
  • grouping
  • aggregate functions
  • HAVING
  • ordering
  • limits
  • projection

It is useful for tests, local demos, small in-memory datasets, and reference behavior.

docs.title: Built-in SQL Compiler
docs.text:
GuardSQL ships a compiler that transpiles a validated AST into parameterized SQL for SQLite, PostgreSQL, and MySQL/Dolt, including JSON path extraction. It is the recommended path for SQL backends and fully realizes the "never execute the original text" principle by regenerating SQL from the AST. See SQL Compiler and Config & Trust Modes.

out, err := guardsql.Compile(q, guardsql.CompileOptions{
    Dialect: guardsql.DialectPostgres, Schema: schema, StrictIdentifiers: true,
})
rows, err := db.Query(out.SQL, out.Args...)

docs.title: Custom Backend Compilers
docs.text:
The built-in compiler covers single-source read queries. For other targets, or for AST features it does not yet emit (joins, CTEs, nested sources), compile the validated and policy-approved AST into your own backend calls:

  • SQL with placeholders and separate arguments
  • Ent predicates
  • DoltDB/MySQL queries
  • PostgreSQL queries
  • API filter structs
  • application-specific query providers

Joins, CTEs, and nested sources are AST-level features. They should be handled by backend-specific compilers that understand the target storage and tenant model.

docs.title: Service-Owned Controls
docs.text:
Backends should always apply:

  • tenant scope outside user text
  • query timeout
  • read-only database roles
  • database row-level security or approved tenant-scoped views
  • service-side maximum rows
  • rate limits and throttling
  • audit logging
  • resource accounting

Do not rely only on user-provided LIMIT.

The database account remains the final boundary for database-to-host RCE risk. Do not grant customer-query execution roles permission to create functions, install extensions, read server files, call network/file/procedure features, or mutate session security state.

docs.title: Output Names
docs.text: Use OutputName(selectItem) to determine projected column names for aggregate and aliased selections. This keeps saved query metadata and dashboard widgets stable across backends.

docs.title: Schema from a Data Catalog
docs.text:
GuardSQL decides which columns a query may reference from each field's Class. Rather than tagging every field by hand, build the schema from a datacatalog catalog, the recommended source of classification. A catalog states, for every field, an explicit visibility (public or internal) and independent pii and secret tags; there is no default, so an unclassified field cannot slip through.

Field.Class is still an ordinary field and can be set by hand for schemas that do not use a catalog.

docs.title: Building the Schema
docs.text:
import (
    "github.com/grokify/datacatalog"
    "github.com/grokify/guardsql"
)

cat := &datacatalog.Catalog{
    Name: "app",
    Entities: []datacatalog.Entity{{
        Name: "users",
        Fields: []datacatalog.Field{
            {Name: "id", Type: datacatalog.TypeNumber, Visibility: datacatalog.VisibilityPublic},
            {Name: "email", Type: datacatalog.TypeString, Visibility: datacatalog.VisibilityPublic, PII: true},
            {Name: "shard", Type: datacatalog.TypeString, Visibility: datacatalog.VisibilityInternal},
            {Name: "api_token", Type: datacatalog.TypeString, Visibility: datacatalog.VisibilityInternal, Secret: true},
        },
    }},
}

schema, err := guardsql.FromCatalog(cat)
if err != nil {
    return err // includes *datacatalog.ValidationError
}
cfg := guardsql.NewUntrustedConfig(schema, guardsql.DialectPostgres)
_, err = cfg.Compile(`SELECT shard FROM users LIMIT 10`) // unknown select field

FromCatalog validates the catalog first and returns its validation error unchanged, so an unclassified field or a secret field that is not internal never produces a schema.

docs.title: Classification Mapping
docs.text:
A guardsql field has a single Class, so when several catalog attributes apply the most restrictive one for query purposes wins:

Catalog field Class Untrusted AllowPII only Trusted secret ClassSecret blocked blocked allowed internal (with or without PII) ClassInternal blocked blocked allowed public, PII ClassPII blocked allowed allowed public ClassPublic allowed allowed allowed

This matches datacatalog's Field.AllowedInQuery(allowPII): with AllowPII false (the untrusted profile) the surviving fields are exactly those for which AllowedInQuery(false) is true, and with AllowPII true exactly those for which AllowedInQuery(true) is true. AllowInternal and AllowSecret admit the internal and secret classes, and are enabled only by the trusted profile.

docs.title: Types and Capabilities
docs.text:
Catalog type FieldType string, unset string number number bool bool time time json json bytes string (guardsql has no binary type)

Every field is Selectable, Filterable, and Sortable, and not Writable. Adjust by name with options; naming an unknown entity or field is an error:

schema, err := guardsql.FromCatalog(cat,
    guardsql.WithWritable("users", "display_name"),
    guardsql.WithNonFilterable("users", "notes"),
)

Entity and field names are lower-cased as by Schema.Normalize; two names that differ only by case are rejected.

docs.title: SQL Compiler
docs.text:
GuardSQL includes a built-in compiler that transpiles a validated AST into parameterized, dialect-specific SQL. This realizes the core security principle: the executed SQL is regenerated from the validated AST, never the original user text.

query text -> parse -> validate -> policy -> Compile -> parameterized SQL + args

Because only constructs the AST can represent — and the emitter knows how to write — can ever reach the database, the compiler is default-deny by construction. Anything else (comments, stacked statements, unknown functions, encoding tricks) is structurally impossible to emit.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
q, err := guardsql.Parse(input)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := guardsql.Validate(q, schema); err != nil {
    return err
}
out, err := guardsql.Compile(q, guardsql.CompileOptions{
    Dialect:           guardsql.DialectSQLite,
    Schema:            schema,
    StrictIdentifiers: true,
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
rows, err := db.Query(out.SQL, out.Args...)

CompiledSQL carries the SQL string and its positional bind arguments:

type CompiledSQL struct {
    SQL  string
    Args []any
}

Most callers use the higher-level Config, which runs parse → validate → policy → compile in one call with secure defaults.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
• Parameterized values. Every literal becomes a bind parameter (? / $1), never string-concatenated. Value-level injection is impossible.
  • Resolved identifiers. Every table and column is re-resolved against the schema and re-quoted per dialect. Raw user identifier text is never passed through; unknown identifiers are an error.
  • Strict identifiers. With StrictIdentifiers (the Config default), every schema identifier must match the unquoted identifier charset. See Trust Modes.

docs.title: Dialects
docs.text: Dialect Constant Identifier quoting Placeholders SQLite DialectSQLite "col" ? PostgreSQL DialectPostgres "col" $1, $2, … MySQL / Dolt DialectMySQL `col` ?

docs.title: JSON Extraction
docs.text:
A field typed FieldJSON in the schema can be addressed with a dotted path. The compiler emits dialect-specific JSON extraction; the path segments are validated as bare identifiers (letters, digits, underscore).

Given payload typed as FieldJSON:

SELECT payload.finding_info.title AS t, count(*) AS n
FROM events
GROUP BY payload.finding_info.title

compiles to:

SQLitePostgreSQLMySQL 
SELECT json_extract("payload", ?) AS "t", COUNT(*) AS "n"
FROM "events" GROUP BY json_extract("payload", ?)
-- args: ["$.finding_info.title", "$.finding_info.title"]

SELECT jsonb_extract_path_text("payload"::jsonb, $1, $2) AS "t", ...
-- args: ["finding_info", "title", ...]

SELECT JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(`payload`, ?)) AS `t`, ...
-- args: ["$.finding_info.title", ...]

JSON path segments may be numeric to address array elements (for example resources.0.uid). JSON values are treated as dynamically typed, so static value-type checks are relaxed for path references. Path segments are limited to ASCII letters, digits, and underscore, matching identifier lockdown.

Postgres extracts JSON values as text, so the compiler casts the extraction to match the query: a numeric literal in a comparison (or SUM/AVG) casts to numeric, and a boolean literal casts to boolean. String comparisons and MIN/MAX are left as text.

WHERE (jsonb_extract_path_text("payload"::jsonb, $1))::numeric > $2

SQLite and MySQL coerce implicitly and need no cast. In Postgres, a JSON value that is not convertible to the target type makes the query fail at execution time; filter such rows out or keep the path's type consistent in your data.

docs.title: Supported Query Shape
docs.text:
The compiler currently supports single-source read queries: SELECT (columns, aliases, and the COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX aggregates), WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, and LIMIT. Joins, CTEs, and nested sources are represented in the AST but are not yet emitted by the built-in compiler; compile them with a backend-specific compiler if needed.

For trusted mutations (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), see Mutations.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This walkthrough shows the recommended way to accept untrusted queries and run trusted mutations end to end. The high-level Config runs the full pipeline — parse, validate, policy, compile — and returns parameterized SQL you hand straight to database/sql.

go get github.com/grokify/guardsql

docs.title: 1. Describe the database as a schema
docs.text:
The schema is an allowlist: it defines what may be queried, each column's read and write capabilities, and its data classification. Capabilities are deny-by-default — a column grants only what you set.

schema := guardsql.Schema{
    Entities: map[string]guardsql.Entity{
        "events": {Name: "events", Fields: map[string]guardsql.Field{
            "id":        {Type: guardsql.FieldNumber, Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true},
            "status":    {Type: guardsql.FieldString, Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true, Writable: true},
            "tenant_id": {Type: guardsql.FieldNumber, Filterable: true}, // used for scoping, not selectable
            "payload":   {Type: guardsql.FieldJSON, Selectable: true, Sortable: true}, // JSON, addressable by path
            "owner_email": {
                Type: guardsql.FieldString, Selectable: true,
                Class: guardsql.ClassPII, // hidden unless AllowPII
            },
        }},
    },
}

docs.title: 2. Accept an untrusted (customer) query
docs.text:
NewUntrustedConfig is read-only, strips secret/PII columns, locks identifiers, and requires a LIMIT. Add a RowScope from trusted session context so the query can only see the caller's tenant.

cfg := guardsql.NewUntrustedConfig(schema, guardsql.DialectPostgres)
cfg.RowScope = guardsql.ScopeEquals("tenant_id", sessionTenantID) // trusted value
cfg.RequireRowScope = true                                        // fail closed

out, err := cfg.Compile(userQuery)
if err != nil {
    return err // syntax error, disallowed field, missing scope, etc.
}

rows, err := db.Query(out.SQL, out.Args...)

Given:

SELECT payload.type AS type, count(*) AS n FROM events GROUP BY payload.type LIMIT 100

out.SQL is dialect-specific, parameterized, and tenant-scoped, and out.Args is ["type", 7, "type"]:

SELECT jsonb_extract_path_text("payload"::jsonb, $1) AS "type", COUNT(*) AS "n"
FROM "events" WHERE "tenant_id" = $2
GROUP BY jsonb_extract_path_text("payload"::jsonb, $3) LIMIT 100

The customer cannot reference owner_email (PII), cannot widen past their tenant, cannot inject via values (bound) or identifiers (allowlisted + charset-locked), and cannot call arbitrary SQL (only the AST is emitted).

docs.title: 3. Run a trusted mutation
docs.text:
NewTrustedConfig permits reads and mutations and full column access. Assignment targets must be Writable; UPDATE/DELETE require a WHERE; and RowScope still applies, so a mutation cannot cross tenants.

tcfg := guardsql.NewTrustedConfig(schema, guardsql.DialectPostgres)
tcfg.RowScope = guardsql.ScopeEquals("tenant_id", sessionTenantID)

out, err := guardsql.Update("events").
    Set("status", "resolved").
    Where(guardsql.Eq("id", eventID)).
    Compile(tcfg)
// UPDATE "events" SET "status" = $1 WHERE ("id" = $2 AND "tenant_id" = $3)

_, err = db.Exec(out.SQL, out.Args...)

docs.title: 4. Layer host controls
docs.text:
GuardSQL secures the query language; the deployment still owns the runtime boundary:

  • a read-only, least-privileged database role for untrusted queries
  • statement timeouts and server-side row limits
  • database row-level security or tenant-scoped views as a final backstop
  • audit logging and rate limits

See Security Hardening for the full checklist and the attack coverage table.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Config & Trust Modes — profiles, classification, row scope, identifier safety
  • SQL Compiler — dialects, JSON extraction, guarantees
  • Mutations — the trusted builder and condition helpers
  • Security Hardening — why it is secure, and what the host must still do

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
GuardSQL is intended to be shared across Grokify and PlexusOne analytics products while keeping product-specific execution outside the core module.

This repository is the Go engine. Integrations that require another runtime should live outside the root Go module. Hibernate support should be implemented in a Java-focused repository such as github.com/grokify/guardsql-java or a more specific github.com/grokify/guardsql-hibernate.

docs.title: UIForge
docs.text:
UIForge uses GuardSQL for Metabase-style Questions and ad-hoc analytics queries.

The UIForge server:

  • reads a neutral analytics catalog
  • converts datasets and fields into a GuardSQL schema
  • asks SystemForge/SpiceDB for dataset and field authorization
  • compiles that authorization into guardsql.Policy
  • checks policy before saving Questions and before executing ad-hoc queries

docs.title: OmniRoadmap
docs.text:
OmniRoadmap exposes product-roadmap analytics over a DoltDB-backed store. It can act as a UIForge analytics provider or expose its own GuardSQL-compatible API.

Recommended boundary:

  • OmniRoadmap owns canonical roadmap data and tenant/product permissions.
  • GuardSQL owns AST parsing and policy checks.
  • UIForge owns dashboard composition and saved Questions.

docs.title: Aha Studio
docs.text: Aha Studio can expose Aha-imported data through a product-specific dialect name such as AQL while reusing GuardSQL internals.

docs.title: VisionStudio
docs.text: VisionStudio can use the same pattern as OmniRoadmap when exposing DoltDB-backed analytics to UIForge or other tools.

docs.title: Dialect Names
docs.text: Product-specific dialect names such as AQL and ORQL can be useful in APIs and UIs, but the shared AST and policy model should remain GuardSQL-compatible.

docs.title: Java and Hibernate
docs.text:
Java/Hibernate should be treated as an external integration target rather than part of the Go engine.

Recommended boundary:

  • The Go engine defines the query language, AST semantics, policy model, and security invariants.
  • A Java module can implement Java-native AST bindings, Criteria/Hibernate compilation, and JVM package conventions.
  • Cross-runtime compatibility should use documented AST/policy semantics and conformance tests instead of importing JVM dependencies into the Go module.

docs.title: Mutations
docs.text:
GuardSQL supports trusted, application-authored mutations (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) through a programmatic builder. Trusted code constructs a statement from typed parts — it does not parse mutation SQL text — and compiles it through the same hardened path as reads: values are bound as parameters, identifiers are resolved against the schema and re-quoted, and the operation must be permitted by policy.

Use mutations only with a trusted Config; customer-supplied SQL must never reach this path.

Assignment targets must be columns marked Writable in the schema (a deny-by-default allowlist, orthogonal to the read capabilities):

"status": {Type: guardsql.FieldString, Selectable: true, Writable: true},
"id":     {Type: guardsql.FieldNumber, Selectable: true}, // read-only, not assignable

docs.title: Builders
docs.text:
cfg := guardsql.NewTrustedConfig(schema, guardsql.DialectPostgres)

// INSERT
guardsql.Insert("users").
    Set("email", email).
    Set("status", "active").
    Compile(cfg)
// INSERT INTO "users" ("email", "status") VALUES ($1, $2)   args: [email, "active"]

// UPDATE
guardsql.Update("users").
    Set("status", "active").
    Where(guardsql.Eq("id", 42)).
    Compile(cfg)
// UPDATE "users" SET "status" = $1 WHERE "id" = $2          args: ["active", 42]

// DELETE
guardsql.Delete("users").
    Where(guardsql.And(guardsql.Eq("status", "disabled"), guardsql.Lt("id", 100))).
    Compile(cfg)
// DELETE FROM "users" WHERE ("status" = $1 AND "id" < $2)   args: ["disabled", 100]

docs.title: Condition Helpers
docs.text:
Build WHERE clauses with typed helpers; every value becomes a bind parameter.

Helper SQL Eq(f, v) / Ne(f, v) f = v / f != v Lt / Lte / Gt / Gte f < v, f <= v, f > v, f >= v In(f, v...) f IN (...) IsNull(f) / IsNotNull(f) f IS NULL / f IS NOT NULL And(...) / Or(...) / Not(e) boolean composition

docs.title: Safety Rules
docs.text:
• Deny by default. A mutation is compiled only if its operation is explicitly listed in the Config's Policy.AllowedOps. A zero Config and NewUntrustedConfig both permit no mutations; only NewTrustedConfig (or an explicit AllowedOps) enables them.
  • WHERE required. Update and Delete reject a missing WHERE unless Config.AllowUnfilteredMutations is set — no accidental full-table writes.
  • Parameterized values. A value such as x'; DROP TABLE users; -- is a bound argument, never inlined SQL.
  • Writable allowlist (mass-assignment defense). An assignment target must be a column explicitly marked Writable in the schema. Writable is deny-by-default, so a caller cannot write a column such as role or is_admin unless the schema permits it — even when the field is readable.
  • Row scope is enforced. UPDATE and DELETE AND the configured RowScope into the WHERE; INSERT stamps the scope's equality terms onto the new row. Columns referenced by the scope cannot be assigned, so a row cannot be written into or moved out of the caller's scope. See Row Scope.
  • Schema-checked identifiers. Unknown columns are rejected; assignment targets must be plain columns (not JSON paths); identifier lockdown applies.

docs.title: Why a Builder Instead of Parsed SQL
docs.text: For internal calls, constructing typed AST nodes is safer than parsing SQL strings: there is no mutation grammar to attack, and the compiler guarantees parameterization and identifier safety. A mutation SQL parser may be added later if routing existing trusted SQL strings through GuardSQL becomes useful.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
guardsql.Policy applies AST-level safety rules. It is designed for structural query controls and for compiled authorization decisions.

For new authorization integrations, call Analyze first and authorize the resulting RequirementSet. CheckPolicy remains the compatibility API for enforcing the current AST-level allowlist.

docs.title: Policy Shape
docs.text:
policy := guardsql.Policy{
    AllowedOps:       []guardsql.Operation{guardsql.OperationRead},
    AllowedEntities:  []string{"roadmap_items"},
    AllowedJoinTypes: []guardsql.JoinType{guardsql.JoinInner, guardsql.JoinLeft},
    AllowedFunctions: []guardsql.AggregateFunc{guardsql.AggCount, guardsql.AggSum},
    Fields: map[string]map[string]guardsql.FieldPolicy{
        "roadmap_items": {
            "name":   {Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true, Groupable: true},
            "score":  {Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true, Groupable: true, Aggregatable: true},
            "status": {Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true, Groupable: true},
        },
    },
    RequireLimit:      true,
    MaxLimit:          1000,
    MaxDepth:          8,
    MaxNodes:          80,
    MaxInValues:       100,
    MaxSelectItems:    50,
    MaxOrderFields:    5,
    MaxGroupFields:    5,
    MaxJoins:          3,
    MaxSubqueryDepth:  0,
    AllowCTEs:         false,
    AllowNestedSources: false,
}

For a generated deny-by-default starting point:

policy := guardsql.SafeAnalyticsPolicy(schema)

docs.title: Read-Only Analytics
docs.text:
Analytics endpoints should normally set:

AllowedOps: []guardsql.Operation{guardsql.OperationRead}

Future mutation operations should remain behind separate APIs, explicit policies, permission checks, and audit logs.

docs.title: Field Policy
docs.text:
When Policy.Fields is configured for an entity, field usage becomes deny-by-default for that entity:

  • selected fields require Selectable
  • aggregate input fields require Aggregatable or an allowed AggregateFuncs entry
  • WHERE fields require Filterable
  • ORDER BY fields require Sortable
  • GROUP BY fields require Groupable, with Sortable accepted for backward compatibility
  • join predicate fields require Joinable when using CheckAnalysisPolicy

SELECT * is rejected when field policy is configured unless AllowStar is true.

docs.title: Structural Policy
docs.text:
Policy can deny or limit:

  • aggregate functions with AllowedFunctions
  • join types with AllowedJoinTypes
  • CTEs with AllowCTEs
  • nested query sources with AllowNestedSources
  • select item count with MaxSelectItems
  • order fields with MaxOrderFields
  • group fields with MaxGroupFields
  • joins with MaxJoins
  • CTEs with MaxCTEs
  • nested query depth with MaxSubqueryDepth

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Policy can enforce:

  • RequireLimit
  • MaxLimit
  • MaxDepth
  • MaxNodes
  • MaxInValues
  • MaxSelectItems
  • MaxOrderFields
  • MaxGroupFields
  • MaxJoins
  • MaxCTEs
  • MaxSubqueryDepth

MaxLimit currently rejects queries with no LIMIT. If a host application wants to allow omitted limits while still applying service-side row caps, it should leave MaxLimit unset and enforce the cap in the backend execution layer.

docs.title: Persisted ASTs
docs.text:
Saving a parsed AST or compiled query metadata can help with audit, query fingerprinting, and repeat execution. It does not replace policy checks.

Always re-check current policy before execution because user roles, relationships, field permissions, and tenant configuration can change after a query is saved.

docs.title: Analysis Requirements
docs.text:
Analyze separates semantic requirement extraction from policy enforcement. This is the first step toward distinct parsed, resolved, authorized, and executable query states.

analysis, err := guardsql.Analyze(q, schema)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

for _, field := range analysis.Requirements().Fields {
    // Authorize field.Entity, field.Field, and field.Usage.
}

Use this layer when mapping GuardSQL to external authorization systems because it records how fields are used, not just whether they appear in a projection.

issues := guardsql.CheckAnalysisPolicy(analysis, policy)

docs.title: Example Policies
docs.text: See examples/customer_analytics_policy.yaml for a human-readable fail-closed analytics profile. The YAML is documentation-oriented; Go callers should build equivalent Policy values directly.

docs.title: Query Language
docs.text: GuardSQL is SQL-like, but it is not SQL. It parses to a purpose-built AST that applications validate and compile into backend-specific execution plans.

docs.title: Basic Query
docs.text:
SELECT id, name, priority
FROM roadmap_items
WHERE status IN ("planned", "in_progress") AND score >= 50
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 25

SELECT is optional. A query without SELECT returns all selectable fields allowed by the backend and policy:

FROM roadmap_items WHERE name CONTAINS "roadmap" LIMIT 10

docs.title: Clauses
docs.text:
Supported clauses:

  • SELECT ... FROM ...
  • WHERE
  • GROUP BY
  • HAVING
  • ORDER BY
  • LIMIT
  • WITH common table expressions
  • joins
  • nested query sources in FROM (...)

docs.title: WHERE Operators
docs.text:
Supported WHERE operators:

  • =
  • !=
  • <
  • <=
  • >
  • >=
  • IN
  • CONTAINS
  • IS NULL
  • IS NOT NULL

Boolean composition supports AND, OR, NOT, and parentheses.

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
Supported aggregate functions:

  • COUNT(*)
  • COUNT(field)
  • SUM(field)
  • AVG(field)
  • MIN(field)
  • MAX(field)

Example:

SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS count, AVG(score) AS avg_score
FROM roadmap_items
GROUP BY status
HAVING count > 1
ORDER BY avg_score DESC
LIMIT 10

In aggregate queries, non-aggregate selected fields must appear in GROUP BY.

docs.title: Joins
docs.text:
Supported join syntax:

  • JOIN
  • INNER JOIN
  • LEFT JOIN
  • LEFT OUTER JOIN
  • RIGHT JOIN
  • RIGHT OUTER JOIN
  • FULL JOIN
  • FULL OUTER JOIN
  • CROSS JOIN

Example:

SELECT parent.id, child.id
FROM roadmap_items AS parent
JOIN roadmap_items AS child ON parent.id = child.parent_id
LIMIT 25

Self joins require aliases on both sources. Duplicate aliases are rejected.

docs.title: CTEs and Nested Sources
docs.text:
GuardSQL can represent CTEs and nested sources in the AST:

WITH active AS (
  SELECT id, status FROM roadmap_items WHERE status = "active" LIMIT 100
)
SELECT active.id
FROM (SELECT id, status FROM active LIMIT 50) AS active
JOIN roadmap_items AS base ON active.id = base.id
LIMIT 10

Nested sources require aliases.

docs.title: Execution Boundary
docs.text:
The in-memory evaluator supports single-source filters, grouping, aggregates, HAVING, ordering, limits, and projection.

Joins, CTEs, and nested sources are parsed and validated as AST features, but they should be executed by backend-specific compilers.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
Use guardsql.Format or guardsqlfmt to normalize user-authored query text. The formatter parses the query first, then emits canonical GuardSQL from the AST.

Multiline output:

SELECT workspace_ref, name, custom.product
FROM initiatives
WHERE provider = "aha-studio" AND workspace_ref = "SAVIN"
PRIORITIZE BY moscow_rice
LIMIT 100

Single-line output:

SELECT workspace_ref, name, custom.product FROM initiatives WHERE provider = "aha-studio" AND workspace_ref = "SAVIN" PRIORITIZE BY moscow_rice LIMIT 100

CLI examples:

guardsqlfmt query.gql
guardsqlfmt --style=singleline query.gql
guardsqlfmt --highlight=ansi query.gql

The Go and TypeScript APIs also support optional ANSI syntax highlighting for terminal display. Browser editors should generally use token spans/classes from their editor component rather than ANSI escape codes.

docs.title: Request Pipeline
docs.text:
Hosted applications should process customer-authored GuardSQL in a fixed order.

Parse -> Validate -> Analyze -> Policy -> Authorize -> Compile -> Execute

docs.title: Parse
docs.text:
Parse converts text into a Query AST. Anything that does not parse is a syntax error, not an injection event.

q, err := guardsql.Parse(input)

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
Validate checks the AST against an allowlisted schema of entities and fields. Validation is structural and schema-oriented. It is not a replacement for user authorization.

err := guardsql.Validate(q, schema)

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
Analyze resolves query sources and fields against the schema and returns the resources, field usages, aggregate functions, and joins needed by the query. This is the preferred input for authorization adapters because it describes what the query actually attempts to use.

analysis, err := guardsql.Analyze(q, schema)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

requirements := analysis.Requirements()

Qualified names resolve through source aliases. Once multiple sources are present, unqualified fields must resolve to exactly one source or analysis fails with an ambiguity error.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
CheckPolicy enforces read-only mode, allowed entities, field capabilities, required limits, maximum limits, expression complexity, and maximum IN list size.

issues := guardsql.CheckPolicy(q, policy)

docs.title: Authorize
docs.text:
Authorization decisions should come from trusted application context, such as tenant membership, RBAC/ReBAC roles, SpiceDB relationships, or service account scopes.

Authorization may be enforced outside GuardSQL, or compiled into guardsql.Policy before CheckPolicy.

For relationship-aware systems such as SpiceDB, prefer authorizing the RequirementSet from Analyze instead of asking one broad question such as "can this principal use analytics?"

docs.title: Compile
docs.text:
Compile only validated and policy-approved AST nodes into parameterized SQL. The built-in compiler targets SQLite, PostgreSQL, and MySQL and binds every value and locks every identifier:

out, err := guardsql.Compile(q, guardsql.CompileOptions{Dialect: guardsql.DialectPostgres, Schema: schema})

Other backends (Ent predicates, API filters, in-memory filters, domain-specific providers) can compile the same AST. Never compile by concatenating user-authored text.

docs.title: One-Step Config
docs.text:
Config runs Validate → Policy → Compile in a single call with secure defaults, and is the recommended entry point for most applications:

out, err := guardsql.NewUntrustedConfig(schema, guardsql.DialectPostgres).Compile(input)

See Config & Trust Modes.

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
Execution should use service-owned controls:

  • tenant scope
  • timeouts
  • row limits
  • rate limits
  • audit logs
  • resource controls

docs.title: Schema Validation
docs.text: GuardSQL schemas define what a query may reference. They are an allowlist, not a database introspection cache.

docs.title: Schema Shape
docs.text:
schema := guardsql.Schema{
    Entities: map[string]guardsql.Entity{
        "roadmap_items": {
            Fields: map[string]guardsql.Field{
                "id":     {Type: guardsql.FieldString, Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true},
                "name":   {Type: guardsql.FieldString, Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true},
                "score":  {Type: guardsql.FieldNumber, Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true},
                "status": {Type: guardsql.FieldString, Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true},
            },
        },
    },
}

docs.title: Field Types
docs.text:
Supported coarse field types:

Type Use string identifiers, labels, enum-like values number integer and floating-point measures bool boolean flags time dates and timestamps json JSON/JSONB documents, addressable by dotted path (see below)

Backends may maintain richer internal types. GuardSQL field types are intended for query validation and UI-safe metadata.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Each capability is an independent, deny-by-default allowlist — a field has a capability only when it is set. This is where per-column access is configured.

Capability Grants Selectable appear in SELECT and aggregates Filterable appear in WHERE Sortable appear in ORDER BY and GROUP BY Writable be an assignment target of an INSERT/UPDATE (see Mutations)

Writable is the mass-assignment defense: because it is deny-by-default and independent of the read capabilities, a caller cannot write a column such as role or is_admin unless the schema explicitly permits it.

"status": {Type: guardsql.FieldString, Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true, Writable: true},
"id":     {Type: guardsql.FieldNumber, Selectable: true, Filterable: true, Sortable: true}, // read-only

docs.title: Data Classification
docs.text:
Each field carries a Class that controls visibility per trust level:

Class Meaning Queryable when ClassPublic (default) ordinary / audit data always ClassPII personal data Config.AllowPII is set ClassInternal platform-only data not meant for customers Config.AllowInternal is set ClassSecret credentials / secrets Config.AllowSecret is set

A field has a single Class. When several sensitivities apply, use the most restrictive: secret, then internal, then PII, then public. A field that is both internal and PII is ClassInternal, so AllowPII alone does not expose it.

Denied fields are stripped from the effective schema, so a query that references one fails as an unknown field without disclosing that the column exists. See Config & Trust Modes.

docs.title: Classification from a data catalog
docs.text: Class can always be set by hand, but the recommended source of classification is a datacatalog catalog, which records visibility, PII, and secret tags explicitly for every field. FromCatalog maps a validated catalog to a Schema so that exactly the fields datacatalog would allow in a user query survive the untrusted profile. See Schema from a Data Catalog.

docs.title: Normalization
docs.text: Schema.Normalize lowercases entity and field map keys and fills missing field names from map keys. Query validation compares names case-insensitively.

docs.title: Dotted Fields and JSON Paths
docs.text:
A dotted name whose base column is a json field is a JSON extraction path. The compiler emits dialect-specific JSON extraction for it, and every path segment is re-validated as a bare identifier:

SELECT payload.finding_info.title FROM events

Qualified source aliases are also supported. Validation only strips known source aliases, so a real dotted field such as custom.launch_tier remains addressable.

docs.title: Semantic Analysis
docs.text:
Analyze uses the same schema allowlist to produce resolved query requirements:

analysis, err := guardsql.Analyze(q, schema)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
requirements := analysis.Requirements()

The requirement set includes:

  • query operations
  • resolved entities
  • field usages such as select, filter, sort, group, aggregate, join, and having
  • aggregate functions
  • joins

This lets host applications authorize exact query requirements with systems such as SystemForge/SpiceDB before compiling or executing a backend query.

docs.title: Security Hardening
docs.text: GuardSQL treats customer-authored query text as an untrusted source language. The engine should accept only the subset it can parse, validate, analyze, authorize, and compile from trusted AST nodes.

docs.title: Why This Is Secure
docs.text:
GuardSQL's safety rests on three principles, not on filtering dangerous input.

Regeneration, not passthrough. The SQL that runs is emitted from the validated AST, never the user's original text. Only constructs the AST can represent — and the compiler knows how to write — can reach the database. There is no grammar for stacked statements, comments, arbitrary functions, arithmetic, DDL, or file/network access, so they cannot be emitted at all. This is default-deny by construction, the same principle as sanitizing HTML by re-serializing it rather than regex-filtering.

Everything is an allowlist. Entities, fields, per-field read/write capabilities, aggregate functions, join types, and identifier characters are all deny-by-default allowlists. A query can only name what the schema explicitly permits; anything else fails validation or compilation.

Values are parameters; identifiers are locked. Every literal is a bind parameter, so value-level injection is impossible. Identifiers — which cannot be parameterized — are resolved against the schema, restricted to a safe charset, and re-quoted, so identifier-level injection is impossible too.

These guarantees hold on the compiled path (Compile / Config.Compile). Using GuardSQL only as a parse/policy gate and then executing the original text verbatim gives up regeneration and weakens the injection guarantees to whatever the parser happens to reject — always compile.

docs.title: Attack Coverage
docs.text:
Strength ratings assume the compiled path (Compile / Config.Compile). Using GuardSQL only as a parse/policy gate and then executing the original text verbatim weakens the injection guarantees to whatever the parser rejects.

  • Strong — prevented by construction.
  • Partial — reduced at the language layer; close fully with host/database controls.
  • Shared — GuardSQL enforces a decision the application must make.
  • App-layer — outside GuardSQL's scope.
Attack class Strength GuardSQL posture SQL injection — values Strong Every literal is a bind parameter; values are never concatenated into SQL. SQL injection — identifiers Strong Table/column names must resolve to a schema field and pass IsSafeIdentifier, then are quoted per dialect. Blind / boolean / timing injection Strong Parameterized values plus no scalar functions or arithmetic in the grammar leave no oracle to build. Stacked queries, DDL, procedures, file/network access Strong Not representable in the AST, so the compiler cannot emit them. Unicode / homoglyph identifier spoofing Strong IsSafeIdentifier is ASCII-only and rejects non-identifier characters. Second-order injection App-layer Values are stored safely as parameters; if other code later concatenates a stored value into SQL, that path is outside GuardSQL. Query-complexity denial of service Partial Policy bounds depth, node count, IN size, LIMIT, and select/join/group/CTE counts; expensive-but-legal queries still need DB timeouts, row caps, and a least-privileged role. Column-level data exposure (secrets / PII) Strong Entity/field allowlist plus ClassSecret/ClassInternal/ClassPII stripping; denied columns read as "unknown field" without disclosing they exist. Mass assignment via mutations Strong Assignment targets must be columns explicitly marked Writable in the schema (deny-by-default), so a caller cannot write a column such as role or is_admin unless permitted; mutations are also trusted-only and reject unknown columns. Full-table UPDATE / DELETE Strong A WHERE clause is required by default; unfiltered mutations are refused unless explicitly allowed. Error-based information disclosure Strong Errors are structural; denied/secret columns surface as unknown fields rather than confirming existence. Broken object-level authorization (IDOR) Strong * The app supplies the trusted scope (session principal → row filter); GuardSQL injects it as a mandatory top-level AND on every SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE via RowScope (and stamps it onto INSERTs, while refusing assignment to scope columns), so no user WHERE can widen it. RequireRowScope makes unscoped access refuse to compile (fail-closed). See Row Scope. Multi-tenant data leakage Strong * Same mechanism: a forced tenant_id predicate is ANDed into every statement, and per-tenant schemas add column-level isolation. Authorization bypass Shared External authz engines compile decisions into guardsql.Policy (authz.PolicyFromDecision); GuardSQL enforces the compiled decision against the AST.

* Strong when the application configures RowScope from trusted session context — GuardSQL enforces the scope but cannot know the session tenant/owner on its own. Without it, row-level isolation is not enforced.

The database account remains the final boundary for resource and RCE risk: run untrusted queries against a read-only, least-privileged identity with row-level security or approved tenant-scoped views.

docs.title: Enforced in GuardSQL
docs.text:
The Go engine can enforce these controls before backend execution:

  • one parsed query, with complete input consumption
  • read-only OperationRead
  • allowlisted entities
  • field usage by operation: select, filter, sort, group, aggregate, join, and having
  • aggregate function allowlists
  • join type allowlists
  • SELECT * denial
  • required LIMIT and maximum LIMIT
  • expression depth and node count limits
  • maximum IN list size
  • maximum select, sort, group, join, CTE, and subquery counts
  • CTE and nested-source denial by default
  • resolved requirement extraction with Analyze

docs.title: Enforced by the Compiler
docs.text:
When you compile with the built-in SQL compiler (directly or via Config), GuardSQL also enforces at emit time:

  • Value parameterization — every literal is a bind parameter, never concatenated. Value-level injection is impossible.
  • Identifier lockdown — table and column names are re-resolved against the schema, re-quoted per dialect, and (by default) required to match the unquoted identifier charset via IsSafeIdentifier. Because identifiers cannot be parameterized, this makes identifier-based injection structurally impossible. See Identifier Safety.
  • Data-classification stripping — fields classed ClassSecret, ClassInternal, or ClassPII are removed from the effective schema unless explicitly allowed, so untrusted queries cannot reference them (and are not told they exist). See Data Classification.
  • Regeneration, not passthrough — the executed SQL is emitted from the validated AST, so only supported constructs can reach the database.

docs.title: Trusted vs Untrusted
docs.text: GuardSQL serves both customer-supplied SQL and internal application SQL from one engine. NewUntrustedConfig is read-only, strips secret/internal/PII columns, requires a LIMIT, and locks identifiers. NewTrustedConfig additionally allows access to classified columns and trusted mutations — still parameterized and identifier-locked. Never use the trusted profile for SQL that originates outside the application.

docs.title: Enforced with Analysis
docs.text:
Use the resolved analysis path for operational systems:

q, err := guardsql.Parse(input)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := guardsql.Validate(q, schema); err != nil {
    return err
}
analysis, err := guardsql.Analyze(q, schema)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
policy := guardsql.SafeAnalyticsPolicy(schema)
if issues := guardsql.CheckPolicy(q, policy); len(issues) > 0 {
    return fmt.Errorf("query shape not allowed: %s", issues[0].Message)
}
if issues := guardsql.CheckAnalysisPolicy(analysis, policy); len(issues) > 0 {
    return fmt.Errorf("query requirements not allowed: %s", issues[0].Message)
}

SafeAnalyticsPolicy is a starting point, not a deployment policy. Host applications should lower or raise limits deliberately and compile current authorization decisions into the policy.

docs.title: Example Policy
docs.text: See examples/customer_analytics_policy.yaml for a human-readable profile that matches the intended fail-closed analytics posture.

docs.title: Host Requirements
docs.text:
Some controls cannot be proven by the AST engine alone. Production systems should also enforce:

  • trusted tenant scope outside user-authored text
  • parameterized backend rendering only
  • read-only database role
  • no DDL, DML, procedure, file, extension, network, or session privileges
  • database row-level security or approved tenant-scoped views
  • statement, transaction, lock, memory, row, and returned-byte limits
  • per-tenant rate limits and concurrency limits
  • cancellation on client disconnect
  • audit logs for original query, normalized AST, analysis requirements, policy issues, authorization decision, and rendered query fingerprint

The database account remains the final RCE boundary. GuardSQL reduces the accepted query language to a policy-approved subset, but it should still run against a least-privileged backend identity.

docs.title: Config & Trust Modes
docs.text:
Config is the recommended high-level entry point. It bundles the schema, the target dialect, data-classification visibility, and identifier safety, and runs the full pipeline (parse → validate → policy → compile) with secure defaults.

Config is JSON-serializable, so an application can load "what the database is and how it may be queried" from a file.

docs.title: Two Trust Profiles
docs.text:
The same engine serves both third-party (customer-supplied) SQL and internal, application-authored SQL. Two constructors provide hardened defaults:

// Customer / Metabase-style SQL: read-only, secret + internal + PII columns stripped,
// identifier lockdown, LIMIT required.
cfg := guardsql.NewUntrustedConfig(schema, guardsql.DialectSQLite)
out, err := cfg.Compile(customerQuery)

// Internal application SQL: reads + mutations, full column access.
tcfg := guardsql.NewTrustedConfig(schema, guardsql.DialectPostgres)
Untrusted Trusted Source parsed query text typed builder (reads: text too) Operations read-only read + INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE Secret / internal / PII columns stripped in the AST accessible Identifiers locked to safe charset locked to safe charset Values bound parameters bound parameters LIMIT required — UPDATE/DELETE WHERE n/a required by default

Trust removes access restrictions, not the safety of regenerating parameterized SQL from the AST: trusted queries are still parameterized, identifier-locked, and schema-checked.

docs.title: One-Step Compile
docs.text:
out, err := cfg.Compile(input) // parse -> check -> compile
// or, to validate without compiling:
q, err := cfg.Check(input)

docs.title: Data Classification
docs.text:
Each schema Field carries a Class:

Class Meaning Queryable when ClassPublic (default) ordinary / audit data always ClassPII personal data Config.AllowPII is set ClassInternal platform-only data not meant for customers Config.AllowInternal is set ClassSecret credentials / secrets Config.AllowSecret is set 
"email":         {Type: guardsql.FieldString, Selectable: true, Class: guardsql.ClassPII},
"password_hash": {Type: guardsql.FieldString, Selectable: true, Class: guardsql.ClassSecret},

Denied fields are removed from the effective schema before validation and compilation, so a query that references one fails as an unknown field — it never discloses that the column exists. This is the automatic AST-step stripping that separates the untrusted and trusted profiles: NewUntrustedConfig allows none of the PII, internal, or secret columns; NewTrustedConfig allows all three.

docs.title: Identifier Safety
docs.text:
Table and column names cannot be bound as query parameters — most drivers only parameterize values — so identifiers are emitted into SQL text. GuardSQL's default defense is a strict charset rather than relying on quoting alone.

IsSafeIdentifier accepts an ASCII letter or underscore followed by ASCII letters, digits, or underscores (up to 128 bytes). It rejects quotes, whitespace, ;, --, and non-ASCII homoglyphs.

guardsql.IsSafeIdentifier("status_id") // true
guardsql.IsSafeIdentifier(`x"; DROP`)  // false

By default (AllowUnsafeIdentifiers is false), Config and the compiler reject any schema whose entity or field names are not safe identifiers — before any SQL is emitted. For databases whose columns are all unquoted-style (the common case), this makes identifier-based injection structurally impossible. Schema.ValidateIdentifiers() performs the check directly.

Set AllowUnsafeIdentifiers only for a database that genuinely relies on quoted identifiers; identifiers are still quoted per dialect in that case.

docs.title: Row Scope (Tenant / IDOR Isolation)
docs.text:
GuardSQL cannot decide whether a principal may see a given row — that needs the session identity and ownership data, which live in the application. But it can enforce an app-supplied decision so it cannot be bypassed. RowScope returns a mandatory predicate for each queried entity, and GuardSQL ANDs it in at the top level of every compiled SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE. Because it is a top-level AND, no user-supplied WHERE — however it uses OR — can widen it.

cfg := guardsql.NewUntrustedConfig(schema, guardsql.DialectPostgres)
cfg.RowScope = guardsql.ScopeEquals("tenant_id", sessionTenant) // trusted value
cfg.RequireRowScope = true                                      // fail-closed

out, err := cfg.Compile(`SELECT id FROM events WHERE status = "open" LIMIT 50`)
// SELECT "id" FROM "events" WHERE ("status" = $1 AND "tenant_id" = $2) LIMIT 50

Even a deliberate widening attempt stays scoped:

-- user input:
SELECT id FROM events WHERE tenant_id = 999 OR id > 0 LIMIT 50
-- compiled:
SELECT "id" FROM "events"
WHERE (("tenant_id" = $1 OR "id" > $2) AND "tenant_id" = $3) LIMIT 50
-- $3 is the session tenant; the mandatory term always holds.

Behavior:

  • Fail-closed on missing column. If a queried entity has no scope column, compilation fails rather than returning unscoped data. ScopeEquals applies to every entity; write a ScopeFunc directly for per-entity columns.
  • Explicit exemptions. A ScopeFunc may return (nil, nil) to exempt a public entity.
  • Require a scope. RequireRowScope refuses to compile when no RowScope is configured, so no query is ever unscoped by omission.
  • Mutations too. RowScope is ANDed into UPDATE/DELETE WHERE (in addition to the required user filter), so a trusted mutation cannot touch another tenant's rows. On INSERT the scope's equality terms are stamped onto the new row (see below).
  • Hidden scope columns. The scope predicate resolves against the full schema, so it may reference a column the caller cannot see, such as an internal-class tenant_id. The user's own query still cannot select or filter on that column.
  • Scope columns are not assignable. Insert and Update reject an assignment to any column referenced by the scope, even if it is Writable, so a row cannot be created in or moved to another scope.

RowScope is per-request session state and is not serialized with Config. Combine it with per-tenant schemas (column isolation) and database row-level security (a final backstop) for defense in depth.

INSERT

An INSERT has no WHERE, so the scope is applied by stamping: each equality term of the scope (tenant_id = 5, or an And of equalities) is added as a column/value pair. A scope that is not a conjunction of equalities (for example IN or OR) cannot be stamped, so the INSERT is refused rather than written unscoped. An entity the scope exempts is inserted unchanged.

docs.title: GuardSQL v0.1.0
docs.text:
Released: 2026-08-22

GuardSQL v0.1.0 is the initial release of the shared query language engine for Grokify analytics services. It establishes the core contract for customer-authored analytics queries: parse user text into an AST, validate it against an application schema, enforce static policy, authorize resolved requirements, then compile trusted AST nodes into backend-specific execution.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Read-only query parser and AST for SQL-like analytics syntax without executing customer-authored SQL directly.
  • Schema validation and policy checks for SaaS-safe reporting, including read-only operation enforcement, field allowlists, limits, expression complexity, and backend planning requirements.
  • In-memory evaluator for single-source analytics queries.
  • Formatter and guardsqlfmt CLI for canonical query display and editor cleanup.
  • Browser-side TypeScript package for UI feedback and query-builder workflows.
  • Optional SystemForge authorization adapter in a nested module so the root Go package stays lightweight.

docs.title: Supported Query Surface
docs.text:
The first release focuses on read-only analytics:

SELECT id, name, priority
FROM roadmap_items
WHERE status IN ("planned", "in_progress") AND score >= 50
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 25

Supported clauses include SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, WITH, joins, nested query sources, and PRIORITIZE BY. Supported aggregate functions are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX.

Joins, CTEs, and nested sources are represented in the AST for backend-specific compilers. The in-memory evaluator currently supports single-source execution.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text:
GuardSQL is designed for hosted SaaS analytics where customer-authored text must not become executable SQL. Invalid input fails as a parse error. Accepted input should still pass schema validation, policy checks, authorization, tenant scoping, row limits, timeouts, and backend compilation using parameterized calls.

For analytics endpoints, applications should normally allow only OperationRead and inject tenant scope outside the user query.

docs.title: Integration Targets
docs.text:
This release is intended to support product dialects such as AQL for Aha Studio and ORQL for OmniRoadmap while sharing the same parser, AST, validation, and policy model underneath.

The next integration work should focus on backend compilers and application schema catalogs for OmniRoadmap, UIForge analytics, and other Grokify reporting surfaces.

docs.title: GuardSQL v0.2.0
docs.text:
Released: 2026-08-23

GuardSQL v0.2.0 is the rename release. The project moved from GrokifyQL to GuardSQL to make the purpose clearer: a SQL-facing safety and policy layer for customer-authored analytics queries.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Project name changed from GrokifyQL to GuardSQL.
  • Go module path changed to github.com/grokify/guardsql.
  • TypeScript package changed to @grokify/guardsql.
  • Formatter command path changed to cmd/guardsqlfmt.
  • Documentation, changelog metadata, MkDocs links, examples, generated TypeScript distribution files, and the optional SystemForge adapter module were updated to use the GuardSQL name.

docs.title: Breaking Changes
docs.text:
This release intentionally breaks import paths and package names.

Area Old New Go module github.com/grokify/grokifyql github.com/grokify/guardsql Go package grokifyql guardsql Formatter command cmd/grokifyqlfmt cmd/guardsqlfmt TypeScript package @grokify/grokifyql @grokify/guardsql SystemForge adapter github.com/grokify/grokifyql/authzsystemforge github.com/grokify/guardsql/authzsystemforge

docs.title: Upgrade Guide
docs.text:
Update Go imports:

import "github.com/grokify/guardsql"

Update Go usage:

q, err := guardsql.Parse(input)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

Update formatter invocations:

go run ./cmd/guardsqlfmt query.gql

Update TypeScript imports:

import { parse, format } from '@grokify/guardsql'

If you use the browser-side parse error type, update GrokifyQLParseError to GuardSQLParseError.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The query language behavior remains the same as v0.1.0. This release is about naming, module identity, package identity, and documentation alignment.

docs.title: v0.3.0
docs.text: This release turns GuardSQL from a parse-and-validate gate into a full transpiler: untrusted SQL in, trusted parameterized SQL out. It adds a built-in SQL compiler, a high-level Config with trust profiles, data classification, identifier lockdown, and a trusted mutation builder.

docs.title: Built-in SQL Compiler
docs.text:
• Compile(q, CompileOptions{Dialect, Schema, StrictIdentifiers}) transpiles a validated read query into parameterized SQL, returning CompiledSQL{SQL, Args}.
  • Dialects: DialectSQLite, DialectPostgres, DialectMySQL.
  • Every value is bound as a parameter; every identifier is re-resolved against the schema and re-quoted per dialect. The executed SQL is regenerated from the AST, never the original text.
  • JSON extraction: a FieldJSON column can be addressed with a dotted path (payload.finding_info.title), compiled to json_extract / jsonb_extract_path_text / JSON_EXTRACT per dialect. Postgres casts the extraction to numeric/boolean for numeric/boolean comparisons and SUM/AVG. Path segments are ASCII-only.

docs.title: Config & Trust Modes
docs.text:
• Config is the recommended entry point (JSON-serializable): parse → validate → policy → compile with secure defaults.
  • NewUntrustedConfig — customer SQL: read-only, secret/PII columns stripped, identifier lockdown, LIMIT required.
  • NewTrustedConfig — internal SQL: reads + mutations, full column access, still parameterized and identifier-locked.

docs.title: Data Classification
docs.text:
• Field.Class of ClassPublic (default), ClassPII, ClassInternal, or ClassSecret.

  • Classified fields are stripped from the effective schema unless AllowPII / AllowInternal / AllowSecret are set; a denied reference fails as an unknown field without disclosing the column exists.

  • FromCatalog builds a Schema from a github.com/grokify/datacatalog catalog, mapping visibility, PII, and secret tags to the single most restrictive Class (WithWritable / WithNonFilterable adjust capabilities). This raises the minimum Go version to 1.25.

docs.title: Identifier Safety
docs.text: • IsSafeIdentifier and Schema.ValidateIdentifiers() enforce the unquoted identifier charset (ASCII, no quotes/whitespace/homoglyphs). On by default via Config and CompileOptions.StrictIdentifiers; opt out with AllowUnsafeIdentifiers. Because identifiers cannot be parameterized, this removes identifier-based injection as a possibility.

docs.title: Trusted Mutations
docs.text:
• Insert, Update, Delete builders compile to parameterized INSERT/UPDATE/ DELETE. Deny-by-default (operation must be in policy); WHERE required on UPDATE/DELETE unless AllowUnfilteredMutations is set.
  • Condition helpers: Eq, Ne, Lt, Lte, Gt, Gte, In, IsNull, IsNotNull, And, Or, Not.
  • Field.Writable (deny-by-default) gates assignment targets — the mass-assignment defense. A caller cannot write a column unless the schema marks it writable, even for a trusted profile.

docs.title: Row Scope (IDOR / Multi-Tenant Isolation)
docs.text:
• Config.RowScope (a ScopeFunc) returns a mandatory per-entity predicate, derived from trusted session context, that is ANDed at the top level of every compiled SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE — so no user WHERE can widen it. On INSERT the scope's equality terms are stamped onto the new row (a non-equality scope refuses the INSERT).
  • The scope resolves against the full schema, so it may reference a column hidden from callers (for example an internal-class tenant_id).
  • Columns referenced by the scope cannot be assigned by Insert or Update.
  • ScopeEquals(column, value) is a ready-made scope for the common tenant_id = <session> case; it fails closed if a queried entity lacks the column.
  • Config.RequireRowScope refuses to compile unless a scope is configured.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: • Existing Parse, Validate, CheckPolicy, Analyze, Eval, and Format are unchanged. Field gains optional Class and Writable; Schema/Entity/Field gain JSON tags. Writable is deny-by-default but only affects the new mutation builder, so there are no breaking changes to the read pipeline.
